An irresponsible decision
Alongside the 1968 German Grand Prix at the
Nurburgring, the 1976 World Championship final
at Fuji is regarded as the Grand Prix that should
never have gone ahead due to the catastrophic
weather. Monsoon-like rain had completely
flooded the track, and the majority of the drivers
refused to line up on the grid.
Aquaplaning, fog and the spray generated by the
wide tyres made a race life-threatening for the
drivers. Yet the officials remained unyielding, as
this was to be the first time a World Championship
final would be broadcast live on television.
After lengthy discussions and delays, irresponsible
officials actually sent the field out onto the track
on that 24 October 1976.

The situation was clear: Niki Lauda, still seriously
injured, led the World Championship in his Ferrari
with a three-point lead over James Hunt in his
McLaren. But the extreme weather conditions at
Mount Fuji turned the race into a pure lottery for
the World Championship - or indeed a battle for
life and death.
Starting from second on the grid, the McLaren
returned from the first lap in the lead. Lauda
dropped far back and, to the horror of the Ferrari
team, retired the Ferrari in the pits on the second
lap. He had only narrowly escaped death a few
months earlier. After several slips, James Hunt
crossed the finish line in third place. A single
point was enough for him to win the 1976 World
Championship.
